reading.body:
Leticia Delgado is named on two AI lobbying filings, both filed through one firm, and those two filings name seventeen separate bills.

The pattern is concentration at the filing level and breadth at the bill level. Two filings carry seventeen distinct pieces of legislation, which means each filing covers many bills rather than one. The client on both is the AFL-CIO, so the AI lobbying here runs through a labor organization rather than a technology company. Every bill listed is dated 2025 or later, so the record covers a single recent window and not a career.

For AI specifically, this is a reminder that the policy layer around compute and data centers is not only populated by chipmakers and cloud providers. Labor organizations file on AI bills too, and a single lobbyist can appear across a wide set of them. Anyone tracking who shapes AI rules has to include filers whose interest is employment rather than hardware.

What this does not show is what any filing actually says. The data gives bill numbers, a client, a firm, and a count. It does not give positions, spending, outcomes, or whether the bills concern AI directly or only mention it. The page states the filings and draws no conclusion about the person, and the reader should not either.
